blocks.text: Separate What You Write from What the Build Produces

A reproducible build needs more than remembering where an executable ended up. We must preserve the source files, project description, selected tools, and options used. CMake lets us describe projects and prepare rules that another tool uses to coordinate their build. First we will distinguish the parts of that process; then we will use them in a real project.

We call the location containing main.cpp and CMakeLists.txt the source directory. The former contains our C++ program; the latter describes its build in the CMake language. The build directory receives generated rules, checks, and resulting artifacts. We choose separate directories to keep these roles distinct; there may also be multiple build directories for the same source files (Scott, 2025, pp. 7–8).

blocks.code:
proyecto/
  fuente/
    CMakeLists.txt
    main.cpp
  construccion/
    ... generated artifacts ...

blocks.text: This tree shows an example layout, not an instruction to move your repository or delete directories. The separation does not depend on these names: a directory named salida does not become source or output just because of its name. What matters is who maintains its files and how they are produced.

blocks.question: You want to change which source files form the program. Where should you preserve that choice so a new configuration can recover it?
options: Only in a rule generated by an earlier build.
In the CMakeLists.txt description maintained alongside the source files.
Only in the name chosen for the build directory.
blocks.explanation: The maintained description is an input to configuration. A generated rule can be produced again; treating an edit to that rule as the only record of a decision loses the link to the source that generated it. Renaming a directory does not select C++ files either.
reviewFeedback: Think about what would happen to that edit when the rules are regenerated from preserved inputs. Check what a fresh build would rely on to recover your choice.
Check that your approach allows the source selection to be recovered from the maintained project rather than from an earlier build's outputs.
Distinguish a directory's name from the contents a tool uses to decide what to build. Explain how that name would preserve the source selection.

blocks.text: Configuring and Generating Are Not the Same as Building Your Application

Configuration interprets the project description, sets options, and checks enabled tools. Generation produces rules for the selected build tool, such as Ninja. A single CMake invocation normally performs both phases, but they serve different purposes. A subsequent build uses those rules to update the required artifacts (Scott, 2025, pp. 8–10).

When enabling C++, project may test the compiler by compiling and linking small test programs. That does not mean our application has already been compiled. A configuration that has not changed may also reuse earlier checks; interpreting a success message requires identifying which step it describes (Scott, 2025, pp. 14–15).

blocks.question: Configuration and generation finished successfully. The target has not yet been requested for building. Which conclusion matches that evidence?
options: The description was processed and rules generated; consulta still needs to be built and its cases executed.
The C++ checks already translated main.cpp; all that remains is to run the resulting program.
Configuration created consulta.exe, although its behavior is still unknown.
blocks.explanation: Success applies to the phases actually performed. It may include internal compiler tests, but does not establish that our program was built, executed, or met its contract.
reviewFeedback: Relate each conclusion to the phase that actually occurred. Check what evidence you have about the requested target and its cases.
Identify which source file the compiler check used and which contains your application. Consider whether you have attributed the same operation to both without verifying it.
Determine which operation would have produced the executable file you mention. Link its existence and revision to a concrete record rather than to a configuration message alone.

blocks.question: A successful compiler check appears during configuration. Which interpretation avoids confusing the phases?
options: It compiled main.cpp; consulta has been updated without requesting its build.
It may have tested the compiler with a helper program; building consulta is still pending.
If the compiler ran, the application has passed its build even before any rules have been generated.
blocks.explanation: Tool checks use their own programs and purposes. They must be distinguished from main.cpp and from the target describing our application.
reviewFeedback: Examine which source file was involved in the compiler invocation. Distinguish testing a tool from updating the target you want to investigate.
Check the purpose of the program used by the check and what work has actually been documented for your own project so far.
Identify the purpose of that compiler invocation before treating it as a complete application build. The presence of a tool in a log does not mean it performed every possible task.

blocks.text: Project, Target, and File Are Not the Same Name

In the next example, CMakeLists.txt uses three commands. cmake_minimum_required declares the minimum CMake version supported by this description: 3.20 is the requirement for this example, not the C++ version. project names the project and enables C++, written CXX in the CMake language. add_executable defines the target consulta using main.cpp (Scott, 2025, pp. 13–15).

blocks.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(consulta main.cpp)

blocks.text: The project is named Existencias, and the target is consulta. By default, the executable file uses the target name with platform conventions: in this example's Windows environment it is consulta.exe. Do not assume the project and the file must share a name. The description shown does not yet specify a C++ standard or all environment options; these choices will also need to be declared when building our working project.

blocks.question: For the description shown, which name identifies the executable target you must request from the build tool?
options: main.cpp, because the source filename identifies the target being built.
Existencias, because project chooses the executable target's name.
consulta, because add_executable defines the executable target under that name.
blocks.explanation: project and add_executable serve different purposes. consulta identifies the target; main.cpp is one of its inputs. The resulting filename also depends on the platform and possible properties.
reviewFeedback: Review the role of main.cpp among the arguments to the command using it. Distinguish a build input from the name used to request an artifact.
Examine what project names and what decision about an executable target you are assigning to it. Justify that connection using the description's arguments.
Relate the chosen name to the role it plays in its command. Then check what you would request from the build tool without confusing the target and its resulting file.

blocks.question: What correctly distinguishes the two files maintained in fuente/?
options: CMake interprets CMakeLists.txt; the C++ compiler translates main.cpp when building consulta.
The C++ compiler interprets CMakeLists.txt and uses it to translate main.cpp.
CMake interprets both files; the compiler merely chooses the name consulta.exe.
blocks.explanation: These are different languages and roles. Adding CMakeLists.txt to a file editor does not mean the C++ compiler interprets its commands. Decisions in that file are only checked when CMake processes it.
reviewFeedback: Track each file: which language does it contain, which tool processes it, and in which phase is it used? Keep those three questions separate.
Examine the syntax of CMakeLists.txt and the kinds of commands you are assigning to the C++ compiler. Check which language that tool is designed to interpret.
Find the program's C++ statements and explain what work must be performed on them to obtain executable code. Review the scope of the compiler's task.

blocks.text: Next we will prepare the files, specify tools and options, configure and generate, build consulta, and run it against known cases. We will preserve evidence of each phase separately and rebuild after making a change. Reading this description prepares those decisions; practical work with the project is an essential part of learning them.
Expressing a Target's Requirements

The previous three commands described the project and its target. We now add two build decisions. This course uses a C++20 profile: the selected toolchain must provide at least the features of that standard. This is a working-environment choice, even if our small practice program does not need all those features.

In CMake, a command has the form name(arguments). In these descriptions, arguments are separated by spaces or line breaks, and parentheses delimit the list. We do not copy the commas between arguments or the final semicolon of a C++ function call. CMake interprets these as build-language commands, while the C++ compiler interprets the source program. Watch the words and argument order: each command assigns different roles to them (Scott, 2025, pp. 12–15).

blocks.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(consulta main.cpp)
target_compile_features(consulta PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
set_target_properties(consulta PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

blocks.text: target_compile_features receives the target name, scope, and required features. Here consulta is the target already created by add_executable; PRIVATE applies the requirement to its own compilation. This word belongs to the CMake language, not to the access specification of a C++ class. cxx_std_20 requests a standard that provides at least the features of C++20; it does not force a compiler to downgrade from a later mode that already provides them (Scott, 2025, pp. 216–217).

set_target_properties assigns properties to targets. Here PROPERTIES introduces the CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF name/value pair: compiler extension mode is disabled for consulta. This property does not prove every program portable or by itself prevent using a library unavailable in another environment. The required standard and extensions are distinct choices (Scott, 2025, pp. 214–215).

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20) sets the minimum CMake version supported by this description and establishes its policy framework; it does not select C++20. The number chosen is not meant to be a universal minimum for any C++20 project. Distinguish the CMake version, C++ compiler capabilities, and target requirements (Scott, 2025, p. 13).

blocks.question: Which line of this description requires at least C++20 features for target consulta?
options: project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
set_target_properties(consulta PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
target_compile_features(consulta PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
blocks.explanation: The feature requirement is attached to the target through target_compile_features. Review which decision each argument expresses before reusing it in another project.
reviewFeedback: Check what LANGUAGES CXX provides. Distinguish enabling a language from requiring a set of its features.
Examine the CXX_EXTENSIONS property you selected. Explain its decision about extensions and what you are claiming about the required features.
Check how the target name, scope, and requested feature relate in the selected command.

blocks.question: The build used a C++ mode newer than C++20 that satisfies the declared requirement. Which conclusion is valid?
options: The minimum requirement may be met by that mode; we did not require exactly C++20.
The build violates the profile because 20 forbids any later mode.
cmake_minimum_required must be changed to the number of that C++ standard.
blocks.explanation: cxx_std_20 expresses a minimum. If a project needs other restrictions, they must be declared and verified; they do not follow from this name.
reviewFeedback: Compare the capabilities of the mode used with the scope of the stated requirement. Keep the CMake version distinct from C++ language features.
Return to what “minimum” means for a feature requirement. Consider what extra restriction you add by treating the number as a prohibition on later modes.
Determine which tool the cmake_minimum_required version applies to before linking it to a C++ language mode.

blocks.text: Calculate the Behavior Before Building

The program decides whether inventory needs replenishment. debe_reponer(disponibles, minimo) must return true when disponibles is less than or equal to minimo. We will use integers with 0 ≤ disponibles ≤ 40 and 1 ≤ minimo ≤ 40. Equality is included in the restocking case: reaching the minimum still requires replenishment.

We will make three calls in this order: (4,5), (5,5), and (6,5). Before looking at an execution, determine what the contract requires for each pair. Here std::cout prints bool values as 1 or 0; we will separate them with colons, without spaces or a trailing newline. boolalpha has not been enabled.

blocks.question: According to the contract, what output should the three calls produce in the given order?
blocks.explanation: Both 4 and 5 satisfy the less-than-or-equal-to comparison against 5; 6 does not. The expected result comes from the requirement, not the implementation we will investigate.
reviewFeedback: Apply the contract's rule again to the equality case. Explain where that call belongs in the sequence of results you chose.
Check each pair separately against the restocking rule. Preserve their order and separators when combining the results.
Check the direction of the comparison between disponibles and minimo on both sides of the boundary. Keep the arguments in each call's original order.

blocks.text: This result will serve as an oracle for these cases: an independent reference against which to compare an observation. Three matches provide evidence about those calls, not proof for every input in the domain. We will also retain which source, description, tools, and steps produced each observation.

blocks.question: An executable produced the expected result for those three calls. What has this directly established?
options: That every input in the domain and every future revision gives the right result.
That configuration alone will correctly execute all future queries.
That this artifact meets the contract for these particular calls and conditions.
blocks.explanation: Link the evidence to the cases actually observed. Other inputs or changed source code need relevant reasoning and checks.
reviewFeedback: Examine which inputs were observed and which revision ran. Justify the leap from those observations to inputs or changes not yet tested.
Identify which action produced the observed output. Review the assumed link between that observation and what configuration alone would do.
Tie your conclusion to the artifact, calls, and specific conditions of the test. Explain what evidence would be needed to extend its scope.

blocks.text: Build and Check consulta in the Lab

This lab preserves two editable files. CMakeLists.txt contains the complete profile description; main.cpp contains the C++ program. The requested target is consulta and the initial build type is Debug. Debug is a build configuration, not proof of correctness or a requirement for the inclusive comparison.

On the phone, CMake uses Ninja and the selected Clang compiler to produce a WebAssembly program that runs with WASI. The consulta.exe file from the earlier Windows example is not the artifact in this Android environment. Check the tools and commands identified in the log instead of inferring them from a filename. This practice requires the CMake profile available for ARM64 and Android 9 or later.

First press Configure / Generate and read its result. Then request Build Target and, only once it finishes successfully, Run Target. Compare the output and exit code with your earlier expected result. The project does not require standard input. Record which phase produced each log: their success messages have different scopes.

projectFiles.initialCode:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(consulta main.cpp)
target_compile_features(consulta PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
set_target_properties(consulta PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

blocks.question: Configuration and building consulta finished successfully. You have not run it yet. What is the next step to check the three calls?
options: Accept the contract as proven because the build completed without errors.
Rename the project before using the built artifact.
Run the current target and compare its output and termination with the oracle.
blocks.explanation: The build produced the program, but you have not yet observed its behavior on these calls. Preserve the link between the artifact and test cases when running it.
reviewFeedback: Identify what the build result establishes about the artifact produced. Review where evidence of its calls' behavior would come from.
Explain what the project name has to do with the behavior you want to check. Before editing it, identify which uncertainty that change would resolve.
Specify what you would observe and which reference you would compare it with. Check that your proposal's cases and artifact belong to the same revision.

blocks.text: For this reference program, execution should print 1:1:0 and exit with code 0. If it differs, first compare the preserved files, target, profile, and logs; an observation can only be attributed to the project that was actually built and run.
A Small Change Needs Fresh Evidence

We will investigate a revision that changes only <= to < in debe_reponer. The CMake description and the three calls remain unchanged. Before building, predict what that implementation will do; keep this result separate from what the contract requires.

blocks.question: What does this revision using a strict comparison print? Predict its actual behavior without substituting the required result.
blocks.explanation: 4 is less than 5; 5 is not less than 5, nor is 6. The change affects the equality boundary: that discrepancy can exist even when the build finishes successfully.
blocks.reviewFeedback: Trace all three calls using the comparison written in this revision, particularly at equality. Then combine their bool results using cout's format, distinguishing what the code does from the original requirement.

blocks.text: The lab starts with that strict revision. Configure, build, and run it to observe its output. Then change only the comparison in main.cpp to meet the contract, and rebuild and run it again. In this simple project, changing C++ source text while preserving its paths and description lets you rebuild using the existing rules. Changing CMakeLists.txt or the profile does require reconfiguration. Do not attribute an earlier result to the new draft.

projectFiles.initialCode:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(consulta main.cpp)
target_compile_features(consulta PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
set_target_properties(consulta PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

blocks.question: The strict revision built successfully and produced 1:0:0 instead of the expected output. What evidence reveals the problem?
options: The functional mismatch at equality, observed in the built revision.
A compilation error, because using < cannot produce a valid C++ program.
Satisfaction of the contract, because exiting with code 0 proves every query correct.
blocks.explanation: A successful build does not decide which comparison the requirement calls for. The second call checks the equality boundary without blaming a phase that did finish correctly.
reviewFeedback: Relate the observed result to the call that tests the boundary. Justify what kind of evidence you are using for the diagnosis.
Distinguish whether you are questioning syntax accepted by the compiler or the meaning of the comparison. Compare your diagnosis with the successful build log stated in the task.
Examine what the exit code reports and what the contract requires for each call. Justify why normal termination would establish the meaning of the results.

blocks.text: Restore the Comparison and Vary the Calls

The fix must preserve the contract's inclusive boundary. It does not change the requirement, the order of the three cases, or the tools merely to make an output match. First complete the function and, after rebuilding that revision, check that the initial cases again print 1:1:0. Once you have that result, vary the calls to test the fix beyond the initial case.

blocks.question: Complete only the comparison operator that preserves the inclusive contract. Do not change names or calls.
blocks.explanation: Equality is included among cases requiring restocking. The less-than-or-equal-to expression represents that requirement with both arguments in their original order.
blocks.reviewFeedback: State in words when restocking is needed, keeping disponibles and minimo in order. Check whether your operator handles cases on either side of the boundary and at equality, without changing the calls.

blocks.text: In your repaired lab, then replace the three pairs with (12,7), (7,7), and (3,7), keeping the correct comparison. First calculate the expected outcomes from the contract; rebuild and compare your observation. You may then restore the initial data. Every revision needs its own evidence: do not treat an old result as if it came from new sources.
Locate a Failure in the Phase That Produced It

CMakeLists.txt is still valid, but main.cpp now contains a syntax error. Identify the complete revision before taking action. Configuration can test the compiler with helper programs without translating this main.cpp; therefore, success at that phase does not rule out an error in the application.

Predict how far this project should get. Configure and generate, then request a build of consulta and read the build diagnostic. Locate the missing semicolon in main's return statement. Fix only that detail, preserve the other files, and rebuild before trying to run. The exact diagnostic may differ across compilers; the file and context matter more than memorizing one message.

projectFiles.initialCode:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Existencias LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(consulta main.cpp)
target_compile_features(consulta PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
set_target_properties(consulta PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

blocks.question: Configuration succeeded, but the subsequent build log reports a syntax error in main.cpp while building consulta. Which action preserves the link between cause and phase?
options: Repeat configuration without changing main.cpp so CMake repairs its statement.
Correct the indicated C++ statement and rebuild the target from that source.
Use the saved result from the previous artifact because the new configuration succeeded.
blocks.explanation: The observed failure belongs to building the revision under investigation. Fixing its source and rebuilding provides new evidence; configuration does not replace that step.
reviewFeedback: Find where the indicated statement is maintained and what repeating configuration without editing it would change. Explain what mechanism would repair that text in your plan.
Identify the source and phase of the diagnostic before planning an intervention. Check how you would link the next evidence to that revision.
Check which version the saved artifact belongs to. Determine whether the failed build updated it before attributing its results to the current attempt.

blocks.text: The reference fix is return 0; at the end of main. After a successful build, run it and verify 1:1:0 and exit code 0 again. If a build fails, do not present execution of an earlier artifact as the failed attempt's result. A file remaining in a directory does not prove that it was updated.
Create the Description Without Immediately Copying a Solution

The final lab contains a correct inventario.cpp with the calls (12,7), (7,7), and (3,7); CMakeLists.txt starts empty. Write a description that supports CMake from version 3.20, names the project InventarioLocal, enables C++, creates comprobar from inventario.cpp, and applies a minimum C++20 requirement to that target with extensions disabled. The requested target is now comprobar, and the build type is Debug. The reference solution is on the next page: try to produce and justify yours before consulting it.

Criteria: the tools must interpret your description; target comprobar must be built from the indicated source; the execution log must belong to that artifact and show 0:1:1 without a trailing newline and with exit code 0. Explain to yourself which decision each command makes and which success you expect in each phase. There is no single valid textual layout: whitespace, comments, and coherent additional commands do not by themselves change these criteria.

blocks.question: Your description creates a target named reserva, but you request a build of comprobar. What should you check before attributing that failure to the C++ in inventario.cpp?
options: That the requested name corresponds to a target created by the current description.
That project receives comprobar, because the project name replaces the target name.
That inventario.cpp is in a directory named comprobar, which would determine the target.
blocks.explanation: Connect the request with the target actually created by add_executable. Program variable names and the project name have other roles; they do not resolve this build request.
reviewFeedback: Relate the request to the names and roles preserved in the description. Find where the artifact to which you attribute the observation is declared.
Distinguish the group named by project from the artifacts you ask to build. Justify why changing that argument would resolve the request you are analyzing.
Explain what build information the directory name supplies in the description shown. Distinguish file organization from the identity you use in the build request.

blocks.text: Compare a Description and Reconstruct the Method

This is a reference solution to the open-ended lab. Compare it with your decisions after making your attempt. Target comprobar is created before requirements and properties are assigned to it; inventario.cpp is a source of that target. Changing all three names requires understanding their roles, not replacing every word with the same name.

blocks.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(InventarioLocal LANGUAGES CXX)
add_executable(comprobar inventario.cpp)
target_compile_features(comprobar PRIVATE cxx_std_20)
set_target_properties(comprobar PROPERTIES CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

blocks.text: A different description may also be valid if it meets the same criteria. It is not enough to make any executable print a fixed string: the program must preserve the function that makes decisions based on its arguments and use it in the specified calls. The exercise is to build the described project and attribute its behavior to it, not to copy an output into the log.

blocks.question: You changed CMakeLists.txt so comprobar uses a different source file that already exists. Which sequence links your next observation to that new decision?
options: Run the program without configuring or building and use the earlier result as evidence.
Configure/generate again, build comprobar, and run the artifact produced from that description.
Build a target with another name without checking the modified description.
blocks.explanation: The description is an input to configuration. After changing it, generate current rules, build the requested target, and check the resulting program.
reviewFeedback: Link the earlier output to the files that produced it. Review what evidence you would have for the change you just saved if you kept only that observation.
For every proposed action, identify which input it uses and which revision it produces. Check that the observation can be attributed to the current files.
Identify what artifact the alternative name represents and why it would reveal the modified decision. Preserve the link between the request and description.

blocks.question: Recall the contract using three new cases at the permitted boundaries. This implementation retains the inclusive comparison: what output do its calls produce in order?
blocks.explanation: 40 equals the minimum 40; zero is below 1; 1 equals 1. All three calls require restocking. The inventory value 0 is permitted: do not confuse it with a minimum of 0, which is outside the domain.
blocks.reviewFeedback: Check the domain of each argument, distinguishing available stock and required minimum. Apply the rule to each boundary pair and combine results in the exact order of cout insertions.

blocks.text: Reconstruct the method without looking at the listing: define behavior and test cases; identify source files, description, and profile; configure and generate; build the target; run and compare; after a change, repeat the affected steps and retain their evidence. The preceding two lessons help distinguish an old observation from an untested hypothesis. In the next lessons, we will apply this relationship to multiple files, dependencies, and project options; this exercise does not pretend to cover those foundations or the entire course.
